slides.title: One question, three hypotheses, one pre-registered benchmark
slides.footer: Take-home: we did not ask 'does the prior work?' — we asked how much of the gain is topology.

slides.title: Bailey et al. 2018, Cell: the recurrence consensus

paper.cite: Bailey MH et al. Comprehensive Characterization of Cancer Driver Genes and Mutations. Cell 173:371-385.
rows: Which genes are mutated recurrently enough across tumour types to be drivers?
9,423 TCGA tumour-normal pairs, 26 tissue types; MC3 consensus of 26 mutation-calling methods; matched CCLE cell lines
A pan-cancer driver catalogue (later the Cancer Gene Census) that became the field's default gold standard
Purely recurrence-based; no network, no prior, and no way to separate a network contribution from the catalogue's own degree bias

slides.footer: Take-home: our label panel is built on this consensus — so we inherit its curation choices and its blind spots.

slides.title: Shi et al. 2025, Nat Cancer: FunMap

paper.cite: Shi Z et al. Mapping the functional network of human cancer through machine learning and pan-cancer proteogenomics. Nat Cancer 6:205-222.
rows: Can a pan-cancer proteogenomic functional network prioritise cancer genes better than existing interactomes?
CPTAC pan-cancer proteogenomics and transcriptomics (published matrices, Zenodo 7948944); machine-learned functional associations
FunMap outperforms STRING for cancer-gene prioritisation; the network is released with a gold standard
Its gold standard is Reactome-derived (>200-protein pathways), and Reactome also feeds STRING's database channel — the paper's own benchmark is partly circular

slides.footer: Take-home: FunMap is both our strongest network and the warning that network benchmarks can be circular.

slides.title: Repana et al. 2019, Genome Biology: the NCG catalogue

paper.cite: Repana D et al. The Network of Cancer Genes (NCG): a comprehensive catalogue of known and candidate cancer genes from cancer sequencing screens. Genome Biol 20:1.
rows: Which genes have been called drivers across published cancer sequencing screens, and how confident is each call?
Curated from the published cancer sequencing literature; confidence levels built on curated PPI channels (HuRI, GTRD, Reactome, STRING experiments)
2,372 cancer genes in three tiers (708 known, 104 candidates, 1,560 screening) with a per-gene confidence level
The confidence level is itself network-derived, and the unlabelled genes are treated as negatives — so it can arbitrate, but not measure

slides.footer: Take-home: NCG is the one catalogue that shares no curation with our labels — which makes it an arbiter, not a metric.

slides.title: What was never measured — and what we predicted
slides.gap: Network-based prioritisation reports large gains, yet no published study separates the topology contribution from node degree and from study visibility (how often a gene has been published about). Standard cross-validation is optimistic when the same protein complexes appear on both sides (Bornigen 2012; Picart-Armada 2019).
hyp: Much of the reported margin is study visibility, not topology.
Falsified if the margin survives a null model that matches positives and negatives on their publication count.
The prior's instability is a property of the gene's own score variance, not of topology, and cannot be smoothed away.
Falsified if any topology descriptor predicts instability, or if a regularised scorer restores the ranking.
Curated networks fail specifically on recently discovered drivers.
Falsified if the failure appears equally on older catalogues.
slides.footer: Take-home: every hypothesis has a prediction that can fail — that is what makes the design worth running.

slides.title: Six networks, five catalogues, one frozen learner
slides.lead: Provenance is an experimental factor, not a nuisance: three protein-derived networks, one RNA-derived, two curated/literature.

RWR frozen at alpha = 0.5 (no tuning) | 5 folds x 40 repeats = 200 evaluations per arm | positive sets capped per network (D-11) | splits fixed and released

slides.footer: Take-home: nothing was tuned after the pre-registration — the design is frozen, and the deviations are written down.

slides.title: From raw public files to a frozen verdict
steps: 6 network edge lists from public releases (FunMap, IntAct, STRING v12, Reactome v86, CPTAC mRNA); harmonise: drop unmapped genes, self-loops, duplicates, keep the largest connected component
5 catalogues mapped to HGNC (D-02: approved symbol wins; aliases only when 1-to-1; ambiguous dropped and counted)
5 folds x 40 repeats per (network, label); positives capped to a common size per network; split files released with SHA-256 manifests
One locked learner (RWR, alpha = 0.5) scored against a degree-only baseline on identical folds; per-gene scores dumped for the gene-cluster bootstrap
Mixed-effects variance decomposition, gene-cluster bootstrap CIs, TOST equivalence, BH-FDR within a pre-declared family
Pre-registration frozen at Zenodo; every departure is an amendment (A2.3a-k, 14 analysis families registered); 50/50 reproducibility checks and 63/63 claim checks pass
slides.footer: Take-home: every number in this talk is re-computable from the public repository.
